summary: Helps 8–9 year-olds see that whole numbers are fractions too: any whole number n equals n/1, and a fraction whose numerator is a multiple of its denominator equals a whole number (4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 6/3 = 2, 6/1 = 6). The core insight grows from iterating a unit fraction — b copies of 1/b make one whole, so b/b = 1 — and is unified on the number line, where 4/4 and 1 sit at the same point. The idea connects informally to division (a/b = a ÷ b). It is designed to address the misconception that fractions are always 'parts' less than one.
misconceptions: 'A fraction can't be a whole number / can't equal 1' — fractions are always 'parts', always less than one
Thinking 4/4 is a little less than 1, or reading it as 'four'
n/1 puzzling — treating a denominator of 1 as meaningless or as zero
Reading 8/4 as separate digits rather than as 2

activities.title: Iterate quarters until a fraction lands on a whole number
steps: Starting from 0 on a number line, add one quarter piece at a time and read the running total: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 …
As the fourth quarter is added, check where the marker lands and name the fraction there (4/4) and the whole number at that point (1).
Keep stacking quarters past one whole and find where 8/4 lands (on 2), noticing it took eight quarters — two full wholes' worth.
Say in your own words how many quarters make exactly one whole, and complete b/b = 1 for quarters (4/4 = 1).
activities.insight: A fraction can land exactly on a whole number: four quarters compose one whole, so 4/4 IS 1, and 8/4 IS 2. This happens whenever the numerator is a multiple of the denominator.

activities.title: A denominator of 1 means 'not cut': writing whole numbers as fractions
steps: Work with whole, uncut bars and read a denominator of 1 as 'the whole is left in one piece'.
Write the number 5 as a fraction (5/1) and explain that it means five wholes, each uncut.
Place 5/1 on a number line at 5, and 3/1 at 3, checking they land on the whole-number marks.
Explain what the bottom number 1 is telling you when you write 3 = 3/1.
activities.insight: A denominator of 1 is meaningful: it says the whole has not been cut, so n/1 is simply n wholes. Every whole number can be written as a fraction.

activities.title: Sort fractions: whole number or not?
steps: Decide for each of 6/3, 8/4 and 5/2 whether it equals a whole number, and sort them into 'equals a whole number' vs 'not'.
For each, test whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, using division: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 8 ÷ 4 = 2, 5 ÷ 2 is not a whole number.
Place 5/2 on a number line to show it lands at 2½, between 2 and 3.
Match 8/4 to the whole number 2 and explain how you knew.
activities.insight: A fraction equals a whole number exactly when the numerator is a multiple of the denominator; a/b can be read as a ÷ b. Having both digits be whole numbers (as in 5/2) does not make the fraction a whole number.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: where does 4/4 land?
steps: Before doing anything, PREDICT with a reason whether 4/4 lands before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 on a number line, and state your reason out loud or in writing first.
Then iterate four 1/4-jumps from 0 (or build four quarters) and observe where you land.
Compare what happened to your prediction, and revise your reason if needed.
State the general rule you now believe about whether a fraction can equal a whole number.
activities.insight: Stating a reason before observing surfaces the belief 'fractions are always parts less than one'; building four quarters that fill exactly one whole and land on 1 contradicts it.

checkQuestion: Is 4/4 equal to 1, or less than 1? Put a dot where 4/4 goes on this 0-to-2 number line and explain why it lands there. Then: which of these are whole numbers — 6/3, 8/4, 5/2 — and how do you know?
checkAnswer: 4/4 = 1 — four quarters make one whole, so it lands exactly on 1. Whole numbers: 6/3 = 2 and 8/4 = 2 (the numerator is a multiple of the denominator: 6÷3 = 2, 8÷4 = 2). 5/2 is not a whole number (5 is not a multiple of 2; it lands at 2½, between 2 and 3).
